title: Ang 1020–1033: Nanak's Solhe
tomorrow: what was there before there was anything at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the riddle of two houses: plenty worries, little wanders, and the one free of both is at ease. More courage. Today, an argument that never gets old.

Subtitles or dubbed? People fight about it over every foreign show. One side says you lose the actor's real voice. The other says you can't follow a story you can't understand. Sikh families have a version of that argument about the Guru's words, and today's pages make it sharp. They hold Guru Nanak's Solhe, long hymns that run on and on, with a rhythm you can feel even before you know what a single word means.
screen: `SUBTITLES OR DUBBED?` → `THE SAME FIGHT, ABOUT GURBANI.` → `LONG HYMNS WITH A PULSE.`

segments.voice: Solhe is read as sixteens: hymns built of sixteen stanzas, here in Guru Nanak's voice, praising the One who made everything and holds it in order. Read one aloud and the length becomes a kind of music, stanza after stanza, the same pulse coming back. Now the argument. One view says: hear it in Gurmukhi. The sounds, the rhymes, the exact words the Guru chose are part of the hymn, and no translation carries all of it. A translation is a window; the original is the room. That's why some families learn to read Gurmukhi even when they speak English at home. The other view says: the point is to understand. People on this side note that the Gurus sang in the everyday speech of the people listening, not in a language only scholars knew. So if the listener now thinks in English, give them the meaning, or the words just wash past. Both sides want the same thing, for the hymn to land. One guards the sound, the other guards the sense. And some sangats do both: the Gurmukhi sung, and a translation shown beside it. Sixteen stanzas, two ways in.

segments.voice: Say one line you know in another language out loud, slowly, a line of Gurbani if you have one, or any line from a song or a grandparent. Then say what it means in your own words. Sit with whichever version stays with you.
